name: Battle of Actium
info: Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa defeated the combined fleets of Mark Antony and Cleopatra off Actium in the Ionian Sea in 31 BCE, after which both took their own lives and Octavian became sole master of Rome.

facts.place: The Ionian Sea outside the straits of the Ambracian Gulf, near Actium in Greece
facts.sides: Octavian, with the fleet led by Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa, against Mark Antony and Cleopatra; 400 galleys against 250 larger ones on the morning, and an estimate of 260 against about 140
facts.outcome: Antony's fleet was routed, Antony and Cleopatra escaped with a few ships, the ships left behind were captured or sunk, and Antony's land army deserted or surrendered.

t: The fleets were of different kinds: Antony's heavy galleys were hard to board but slow, and Octavian's smaller Liburnian vessels could get in close, attack the crews and retreat.
Antony's side was weakened before the fighting began by desertion, disease and a severe malaria outbreak, and by the defection of his general Quintus Dellius with his battle plans.
Historians generally view the consolidation of power that followed as the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire.
dyk: Antony came to Actium with around 500 ships but could not man all of them, and for the battle itself it is estimated that he had around 140 ships against Octavian's 260.
ev: The Second Triumvirate is renewed for five years at Tarentum
Antony and Cleopatra raise Caesarion to power with the title King of the Kings
Antony divorces Octavia and goes to Ephesus with Cleopatra, and Rome declares war on Cleopatra
Antony's forces are blockaded at Actium while Agrippa raids the Greek coast
Antony's fleet sails out of the straits and is routed by Octavian's fleet
Antony is beaten at Alexandria and dies, and Cleopatra kills herself
Octavian founds Nicopolis to commemorate the victory
The Senate awards Octavian the title Augustus

sections.background:
The Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus was renewed for five years at Tarentum in 37 BCE. It broke down when Octavian came to see Caesarion, the professed son of Julius Caesar and Cleopatra VII of Egypt, as a major threat, and when Antony abandoned his wife Octavia Minor, Octavian's sister, and moved to Egypt. Octavian's standing rested on Caesar's legacy of 44 BCE, which made him Caesar's adopted son and heir, while Antony had been Caesar's most successful senior officer and claimed much of the support of Caesar's soldiers and veterans.

In 34 BCE Antony and Cleopatra raised Caesarion, then 13, to power with the title King of the Kings. Octavian began a propaganda war, denouncing Antony as an enemy of Rome who intended to set up a monarchy on Caesarion's behalf and move the capital to Alexandria. Each man also had specific complaints against the other. The triumvirate expired on the last day of 33 BCE.

In 32 BCE one third of the Senate and both consuls, Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Gaius Sosius, joined Antony. He divorced Octavia and went to Ephesus with Cleopatra, where a vast fleet gathered, a large proportion of it furnished by her. Octavian obtained Antony's deposition from the consulship of 31 BCE and a proclamation of war against Cleopatra, which was understood to mean Antony.
sections.forces:
Figures differ. In early 31 BCE Antony is said to have had 500 ships and 70,000 infantry and Octavian 400 ships and 80,000 infantry. On the morning of 2 September Antony is credited with 250 larger galleys with towers full of armed men and Octavian 400 galleys, and another estimate gives Antony around 140 ships against 260 for Octavian. Antony had arrived with around 500 ships but could not man them all. Plutarch and Dio speak of desertion and disease in his camp, and many ships were short of rowers after a severe malaria outbreak.

Antony's ships were mainly quinqueremes with smaller quadriremes, heavier and wider than Octavian's. His flagship was a ten, and an eight carried around 200 heavy marines, archers and at least six ballistae. They were very difficult to board but less manoeuvrable. Octavian's fleet was largely of smaller Liburnian vessels, with better trained, well-fed and rested crews.

Agrippa commanded Octavian's left wing, Lucius Arruntius the centre and Marcus Lurius the right, while Titus Statilius Taurus commanded the army on the shore north of the straits. Antony and Lucius Gellius Poplicola held Antony's right wing, Marcus Octavius and Marcus Insteius the centre and Gaius Sosius the left, with Cleopatra's squadron behind. Publius Canidius Crassus commanded the land forces. Before the battle Quintus Dellius defected to Octavian with Antony's battle plans.
sections.course:
Antony had first planned a descent on Italy at the end of 32 BCE but found the sea guarded and wintered at Patrae, with his fleet in the Ambracian Gulf and his army near the promontory of Actium. In 31 BCE Agrippa raided Greek towns along the coast and Octavian's cavalry won skirmishes, so that Antony confined his soldiers to the southern camp. Cleopatra advised garrisoning strong towns and returning the main fleet to Alexandria, and this was apparently agreed. Octavian first considered letting Antony sail and then attacking him, but Agrippa persuaded him to give battle.

On 1 September Octavian addressed his fleet. The next day was wet and the sea rough. Antony's fleet came out of the straits and formed a line and remained quiet. Octavian ordered his ships to steer right and pass the enemy, and Antony, fearing to be surrounded, gave the word to attack. Antony had hoped to drive back Agrippa's wing with his biggest ships, but Octavian's fleet, aware of this, stayed out of range. The battle raged all afternoon without a decisive result.

Cleopatra's fleet in the rear then retreated to the open sea without engaging. Antony, who had not observed the signal, believed all was lost and followed. Many ships raised sail and threw their towers overboard. Some fought on until long after nightfall, when many were blazing from firebrands. Antony burned the ships he could no longer man, transferred to a smaller vessel and escaped with a few ships. Those left behind were captured or sunk.
sections.aftermath:
Octavian spent the night on board saving the crews of the burning vessels. The next day Antony's camp was occupied. Under cover of darkness some 19 legions and 12,000 cavalry had fled before Antony could fight a land battle, and the army that had been equal to Octavian's deserted. Octavian visited Greece and Asia and wintered at Samos, though he had to go briefly to Brundisium to settle a mutiny and arrange land assignments.

At Samos he received a message from Cleopatra with a gold crown and throne, offering to abdicate in favour of her sons. In spring Cornelius Gallus advanced from Paraetonium and Octavian landed at Pelusium. Antony was defeated by Gallus and, after a minor victory at Alexandria on 31 July 30 BCE, was decisively beaten in a general attack. Believing false rumours that Cleopatra had killed herself, he stabbed himself in the stomach, and died in her arms in the mausoleum where she was hiding.

Cleopatra killed herself on 12 August 30 BCE. Octavian had Caesarion killed later that month, and also Antony's elder son Antyllus, but spared the children of Antony and Cleopatra. He gave Antony and Cleopatra a public military funeral in Rome. Egypt became a Roman province, ending the Ptolemaic Kingdom and the Hellenistic Period.
sections.sources:
Plutarch and Dio record the desertion and disease that plagued Antony's camp. In the traditional narrative of the battle Cleopatra's squadron retreats and Antony follows it. Lange argues that Antony would have had victory within reach were it not for Cleopatra's retreat.

J. M. Carter gives a differing account. In it Antony knew he was surrounded and gathered his ships in a quasi-horseshoe close to the shore. He then sent the northern ships out to attack, had Sosius spread the southern ones, and with Cleopatra sped through the gap left in Octavian's formation, abandoning his entire force. That reading makes the escape Antony's plan and not a flight.

The figures for the fleets disagree: 500 ships for Antony and 400 for Octavian early in the year, 250 and 400 on the morning of the battle, and an estimate of 140 against 260. Octavian's victory at Alexandria is dated either 31 July or 1 August 30 BCE. Pelling notes that two former consuls commanded Antony's wings, which suggests that the major action was expected there. A suggestion by scientists researching the dead water phenomenon is that the Egyptian fleet may have been trapped in dead water, which can substantially reduce a ship's speed.
sections.legacy:
Octavian's victory gave him sole, uncontested control of Mare Nostrum, the Roman Mediterranean, and consolidated his power over every Roman institution. He adopted the title Princeps, first citizen, and in 27 BCE the Senate awarded him the title Augustus. He kept the trappings of a restored Republican leader, but historians generally view his consolidation of power and his honorifics as the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire.

To commemorate the victory Octavian founded the city of Nicopolis, City of Victory, in 29 BCE on the southernmost promontory of Epirus, opposite Actium. On a hill just north of it, where he had made his camp, he built the Campsite Memorial, a tropaion dedicated to Neptune, Mars and Apollo, which displayed bronze rams taken from captured warships. At the cape of Actium he built the Actian dekanaia, a tropaion made of ten captured warships. The Temple of Apollo Aktios, a deity Octavian repeatedly invoked after the war, was renovated and enlarged.

Octavian's triple triumph on his return to Rome, spread over three days, celebrated his victory over Illyria, the Battle of Actium and his conquest of Egypt. He was given credit for pardoning many of his opponents after the battle, although he had previously shown little mercy to surrendered enemies.

summary: At Actium on 2 September 31 BCE the fleet of Octavian under Agrippa routed the fleets of Antony and Cleopatra, who escaped with a few ships. Antony's army deserted, both leaders died the next year, and Octavian emerged as sole ruler of Rome.
references: Robert Alan Gurval, Actium and Augustus: The Politics and Emotions of Civil War (University of Michigan Press, 1995)
Si Sheppard, Actium 31 BC: Downfall of Antony and Cleopatra (Osprey Publishing, 2009)
David J. Califf, Battle of Actium (Chelsea House Publishers, 2004)
notes: Strength figures conflict inside the article: 500 ships and 70,000 infantry (Antony) against 400 ships and 80,000 infantry (Octavian) early in 31 BCE; 250 larger galleys against 400 in the order of battle; an estimate of 140 against 260 in the combat section. I gave all three and did not choose.
Date of Octavian's victory at Alexandria: 1 August 30 BCE in the introduction, 31 July 30 BCE in the aftermath. I gave 31 July in the aftermath text and the sources section names both.
The article says the battle raged 'by about noon' and 'shortly after midday' the line was extended; I left the exact hour out.

The article's text on the fighting is partly internally inconsistent (Octavian's fleet is said to put to sea after Antony extends his line, yet also to be waiting beyond the straits); I kept to the sequence of the 'Battle' section.

The article names almost no ancient sources for the course (Plutarch and Dio only for desertion); the sources section is therefore thin and says so. The editor may wish to add Velleius, Livy tradition or Virgil from a second source.

The article says Octavian's funeral for Antony and Cleopatra was partly due to respect and partly to show his benevolence; I gave only the funeral. The article also says Octavian 'admired the bravery of Cleopatra'; left out.

Left out: the weapons details of the harpax, ballista ranges, the Antony will and Plancus, Donations details beyond the title, Antony's offers to Octavian from Egypt, the Dellius detail beyond defection.
The Antony's-ships passage says his eight carried about 200 marines; the article says 'An eight war galley', I wrote it as given.
